narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 53.4% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Both placed you in the bottom decile of your school, far below the average of roughly sixth decile among students who were accepted. This low academic standing in law school was the main reason the model doubted your likelihood of passing the bar.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.40 worked in the opposite direction. It is higher than the 3.23 average of accepted students and therefore pulled the prediction toward success, but not enough to overcome the effect of your law-school class rank.

Your family income bracket of upper-middle class also nudged the outcome slightly toward passing. Among accepted applicants, upper-middle income is the most common category, so this was viewed as a mild positive.

Taken together, the model concluded your current academic performance in law school made success on the bar exam uncertain. To improve your chances, you should focus on raising your class rank through targeted study, seek academic support from your school, and consider retaking the LSAT or strengthening other parts of your profile before reapplying.
